401(K)/RETIREMENT PLAN DISTRIBUTION NOTICE AT TERMINATION
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

DECLARATION AND SCOPE OF THIS NOTICE
This 401(k)/Retirement Plan Distribution Notice at Termination concerns Jordan Lee, whose employment with Acme, Inc. ended on October 1, 2026, and Jordan Lee's account under Acme, Inc.'s Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan. It states general rules of federal law that govern what happens to a former employee's account balance under an employer-sponsored retirement plan such as a 401(k) once employment ends: the tax treatment available for a distribution from the plan, the right to have a distribution transferred directly to another eligible retirement plan, the mandatory withholding that applies when a distribution is instead paid to the former employee, the plan administrator's obligation to explain these rules in writing before making a distribution, and the vesting rules that determine what portion of the account balance is the former employee's to keep. This notice states rules of general federal law. It does not state the terms of Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan itself, which can vary within what federal law permits, and it does not state what Jordan Lee should do about any distribution, rollover, or election.

TAX-FREE ROLLOVER OF AN ELIGIBLE ROLLOVER DISTRIBUTION WITHIN 60 DAYS
Federal tax law allows an "eligible rollover distribution" from a qualified retirement plan to be excluded from an employee's gross income for the year paid, if the recipient transfers the distributed property to an eligible retirement plan such as an IRA or another qualified employer plan. That transfer generally must happen no later than the 60th day after the day the distributee received the distributed property, subject to a narrow hardship waiver of that 60-day rule that the Secretary of the Treasury may grant. Whether a distribution Jordan Lee receives from Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan qualifies as an eligible rollover distribution in the first place, and whether a transfer of it is completed within the applicable time limit, are separate questions this clause does not resolve for Jordan Lee's specific distribution.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If— (A) any portion of the balance to the credit of an employee in a qualified trust is paid to the employee in an eligible rollover distribution, (B) the distributee transfers any portion of the property received in such distribution to an eligible retirement plan, and (C) in the case of a distribution of property other than money, the amount so transferred consists of the property distributed, then such distribution (to the extent so transferred) shall not be includible in gross income for the taxable year in which paid."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, exclusion from income for a rolled-over eligible rollover distribution (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/402)
  "Except as provided in subparagraphs (B) and (C), paragraph (1) shall not apply to any transfer of a distribution made after the 60th day following the day on which the distributee received the property distributed."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, 60-day time limit on rollover transfers (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/402)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the general tax-free-rollover mechanism and the 60-day time limit under 26 U.S.C. § 402(c) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs the reader's situation, and not a claim about the terms of any specific retirement plan, which can vary within what federal law permits. This clause is not a claim about whether any particular distribution qualifies as an eligible rollover distribution (a separate clause in this document addresses that definition) or about whether the Secretary would grant a hardship waiver of the 60-day rule in any specific case. Both citations below are to different subsections of the same statutory section, 26 U.S.C. § 402(c) — paragraph (1) (the exclusion-from-income rule) and paragraph (3)(A) (the 60-day time limit) — and are disclosed together here rather than presented as independent sources.

WHAT COUNTS AS AN "ELIGIBLE ROLLOVER DISTRIBUTION" UNDER FEDERAL TAX LAW
Not every payment out of a qualified retirement plan is an "eligible rollover distribution." Federal tax law defines the term broadly, as any distribution to an employee of all or any portion of the balance credited to the employee in a qualified trust, but then carves out three specific categories that are not eligible rollover distributions: (1) a distribution that is one of a series of substantially equal periodic payments made at least annually, for the life or life expectancy of the employee (or the joint lives or joint life expectancies of the employee and a designated beneficiary), or for a specified period of 10 years or more; (2) a distribution required under the federal minimum-distribution rules; and (3) a distribution made on account of the employee's hardship. Whether a specific payment Jordan Lee may receive from Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan falls within the general definition or within one of these three carve-outs depends on the nature of that specific payment, which this clause does not determine.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "For purposes of this subsection, the term “eligible rollover distribution” means any distribution to an employee of all or any portion of the balance to the credit of the employee in a qualified trust; except that such term shall not include— (A) any distribution which is one of a series of substantially equal periodic payments (not less frequently than annually) made— (i) for the life (or life expectancy) of the employee or the joint lives (or joint life expectancies) of the employee and the employee's designated beneficiary, or (ii) for a specified period of 10 years or more, (B) any distribution to the extent such distribution is required under section 401(a)(9), and (C) any distribution which is made upon hardship of the employee."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(4) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, definition of "eligible rollover distribution" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/402)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the statutory definition of "eligible rollover distribution" and its three carve-outs under 26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(4) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs the reader's situation, and not a claim about the terms of any specific retirement plan, which can vary within what federal law permits. This clause cites a single statutory paragraph (§ 402(c)(4)); it does not restate the separate 2020-specific transition rule that appears later in the same paragraph, which is no longer of current relevance and was not carried into this clause's body text.

THE RIGHT TO A DIRECT ROLLOVER TO ANOTHER ELIGIBLE RETIREMENT PLAN
Separately from the tax-free-rollover mechanism itself, federal tax law imposes a qualification requirement on the plan: a trust cannot be a "qualified trust" — meaning the tax-favored retirement plan status Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan depends on — unless the plan gives a distributee who is entitled to an eligible rollover distribution the option to have that distribution paid directly to an eligible retirement plan the distributee specifies, made as a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer, rather than paid to the distributee first. This direct-rollover option is what allows a distributee to receive an eligible rollover distribution without the distribution passing through the distributee's own hands at all.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A trust shall not constitute a qualified trust under this section unless the plan of which such trust is a part provides that if the distributee of any eligible rollover distribution— (i) elects to have such distribution paid directly to an eligible retirement plan, and (ii) specifies the eligible retirement plan to which such distribution is to be paid (in such form and at such time as the plan administrator may prescribe), such distribution shall be made in the form of a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer to the eligible retirement plan so specified."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 401(a)(31)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, qualified-trust requirement to offer a direct rollover (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/401)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the statutory direct-rollover requirement under 26 U.S.C. § 401(a)(31)(A) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs the reader's situation, and not a claim about the terms of any specific retirement plan, which can vary within what federal law permits. This clause cites a single statutory subparagraph (§ 401(a)(31)(A)); it does not restate the separate automatic-cash-out / mandatory-distribution rule in the neighboring subparagraph (§ 401(a)(31)(B)), which applies only to certain small mandatory distributions and is not addressed in this document.

MANDATORY 20% WITHHOLDING WHEN A DISTRIBUTION IS PAID DIRECTLY TO THE EMPLOYEE
If an eligible rollover distribution is paid to the distributee rather than transferred directly to an eligible retirement plan, federal tax law requires the payor to withhold federal income tax from the distribution at a mandatory rate of 20 percent, regardless of the distributee's actual income tax liability for the year. This mandatory 20% withholding does not apply, however, to any distribution that the distributee elects to have paid directly to an eligible retirement plan under the direct-rollover provision described elsewhere in this document. In other words, the 20% withholding is specifically tied to the choice between a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer and a payment made to the distributee personally.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In the case of any designated distribution which is an eligible rollover distribution— (A) subsections (a) and (b) shall not apply, and (B) the payor of such distribution shall withhold from such distribution an amount equal to 20 percent of such distribution."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 3405(c)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, mandatory 20% withholding on an eligible rollover distribution (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/3405)
  "Paragraph (1)(B) shall not apply to any distribution if the distributee elects under section 401(a)(31)(A) to have such distribution paid directly to an eligible retirement plan."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 3405(c)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, exception for a direct rollover election (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/3405)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the mandatory 20% withholding rule and its direct-rollover exception under 26 U.S.C. § 3405(c) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs the reader's situation, and not a claim about the terms of any specific retirement plan, which can vary within what federal law permits, and not a claim about any specific reader's actual federal income tax liability, which this withholding amount does not determine. Both citations below are to different subsections of the same statutory section, 26 U.S.C. § 3405(c) — paragraph (1) (the 20%-withholding rule) and paragraph (2) (the direct-rollover exception) — and are disclosed together here rather than presented as independent sources.

THE PLAN ADMINISTRATOR'S WRITTEN EXPLANATION BEFORE A DISTRIBUTION: THE SECTION 402(F) NOTICE
Before making an eligible rollover distribution, federal tax law itself — not merely a regulation implementing it — requires the plan administrator to give the recipient a written explanation covering: the recipient's right to have the distribution directly transferred to an eligible retirement plan (and that automatic direct transfer applies to certain distributions); the withholding of tax that applies if the distribution is not directly transferred; the conditions under which the distribution will not be taxed if transferred to an eligible retirement plan within 60 days of receipt; certain special tax-computation provisions, where applicable; and the fact that the receiving plan may impose restrictions or tax consequences different from those of the distributing plan. This written explanation is commonly referred to as a "402(f) notice," after the Internal Revenue Code section that requires it, and it must be provided within a reasonable period of time before the distribution is made.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The plan administrator of any plan shall, within a reasonable period of time before making an eligible rollover distribution, provide a written explanation to the recipient— (A) of the provisions under which the recipient may have the distribution directly transferred to an eligible retirement plan and that the automatic distribution by direct transfer applies to certain distributions in accordance with section 401(a)(31)(B), (B) of the provision which requires the withholding of tax on the distribution if it is not directly transferred to an eligible retirement plan, (C) of the provisions under which the distribution will not be subject to tax if transferred to an eligible retirement plan within 60 days after the date on which the recipient received the distribution, (D) if applicable, of the provisions of subsections (d) and (e) of this section, and (E) of the provisions under which distributions from the eligible retirement plan receiving the distribution may be subject to restrictions and tax consequences which are different from those applicable to distributions from the plan making such distribution."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 402(f)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, written explanation before an eligible rollover distribution (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/402)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the written-explanation requirement under 26 U.S.C. § 402(f)(1) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs the reader's situation, and not a claim about the terms of any specific retirement plan, which can vary within what federal law permits. This clause cites a single statutory paragraph (§ 402(f)(1)); it does not address the separate cross-referenced provisions of §§ 402(d) or (e), which the notice must also cover "if applicable" but which are not otherwise addressed in this document. This requirement is set out directly in the Internal Revenue Code itself, at 26 U.S.C. § 402(f) — it is not solely a creature of Treasury regulations, and this clause does not rely on, or cite, 29 U.S.C. § 1132 (ERISA's civil-enforcement provision), which is a different statute addressing who may sue to enforce ERISA rights rather than the content of this notice.

VESTING: EMPLOYEE CONTRIBUTIONS ARE ALWAYS FULLY VESTED; EMPLOYER CONTRIBUTIONS MAY VEST ON A SCHEDULE
Federal law draws a sharp line between two sources of money inside a retirement plan account like Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan. An employee's own contributions to the plan — such as elective deferrals from Jordan Lee's own pay — are always fully, immediately nonforfeitable ("vested"): federal law requires that a plan treat an employee's rights in the portion of the account derived from the employee's own contributions as nonforfeitable, with no waiting period at all. Employer contributions, such as an employer match or profit-sharing contribution, are different: federal law permits a plan to vest that portion of the account on a schedule instead of immediately. For a 401(k) or similar individual-account (defined-contribution) plan specifically, federal law permits, at most, a schedule under which an employee becomes 100% vested in employer contributions after completing 3 years of service (with nothing vested before that point), or, alternatively, a graded schedule of at least 20% after 2 years of service, 40% after 3, 60% after 4, 80% after 5, and 100% after 6 years of service. A plan may vest employer contributions faster than these schedules — including immediately — but federal law does not allow a 401(k)-type plan to vest more slowly than whichever of these two schedules it has adopted. Whether Jordan Lee's specific account under Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan uses the 3-year-cliff schedule, the graded schedule, faster vesting, or some other permitted combination, and how many years of vesting service Jordan Lee had completed as of October 1, 2026, are questions this clause does not answer; they depend on Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan's own terms and Jordan Lee's own service record.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A plan satisfies the requirements of this paragraph if an employee's rights in his accrued benefit derived from his own contributions are nonforfeitable."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1053(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, full vesting of an employee's own contributions (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/1053)
  "(i) In the case of an individual account plan, a plan satisfies the requirements of this paragraph if it satisfies the requirements of clause (ii) or (iii). (ii) A plan satisfies the requirements of this clause if an employee who has completed at least 3 years of service has a nonforfeitable right to 100 percent of the employee's accrued benefit derived from employer contributions. (iii) A plan satisfies the requirements of this clause if an employee has a nonforfeitable right to a percentage of the employee's accrued benefit derived from employer contributions determined under the following table: Years of service: The nonforfeitable percentage is: 2 20 3 40 4 60 5 80 6 or more 100."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1053(a)(2)(B) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, maximum permitted vesting schedules for an individual account plan (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/1053)
  "The term “individual account plan” or “defined contribution plan” means a pension plan which provides for an individual account for each participant and for benefits based solely upon the amount contributed to the participant's account, and any income, expenses, gains and losses, and any forfeitures of accounts of other participants which may be allocated to such participant's account."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1002(34) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, definition of "individual account plan" / "defined contribution plan" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/1002)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the vesting rules under 29 U.S.C. § 1053(a) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs the reader's situation, and not a claim about the terms of any specific retirement plan, which can vary within what federal law permits. Two of the citations below are to different subsections of the same statutory section, 29 U.S.C. § 1053(a) — paragraph (1) (full vesting of an employee's own contributions) and paragraph (2)(B) (the two permitted maximum vesting schedules for an individual account plan) — and are disclosed together here rather than presented as independent sources. This clause states the individual-account-plan vesting schedules in § 1053(a)(2)(B), because a 401(k) is an individual account (defined contribution) plan; § 1053(a)(2)(A), a separate, slightly longer schedule (a 5-year cliff, or a 3-through-7-year graded schedule) that applies specifically to defined benefit plans, is not restated here because it does not govern a 401(k)-type account. The third citation, to 29 U.S.C. § 1002(34), a different statutory section defining "individual account plan," supports that classification and is cited as a separate, independent source rather than folded into the § 1053(a) disclosure above.

STATEMENT OF PLAN AND ACCOUNT INFORMATION, AND SIGNATURE
The following information relates to Jordan Lee's account under Acme, Inc.'s Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan following the termination of Jordan Lee's employment on October 1, 2026:

Retirement plan name: Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan

Vested account balance (if known as of the date of this notice): $18,450.00

This document does not state, and should not be read to state, whether Jordan Lee should roll this balance over, take it as a cash distribution, leave it in Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan (if the plan permits that), or take any other action available under Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan's own terms and applicable federal law. Those are decisions for Jordan Lee to make, informed by the written explanation Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan's administrator is required to provide before any eligible rollover distribution is made, and by Jordan Lee's own tax and financial considerations, which this document does not address.

Jordan Lee states that the foregoing plan and balance information is accurate to the best of Jordan Lee's knowledge as of the date below.

Signature: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

Jordan Lee

citations.quote: A plan satisfies the requirements of this paragraph if an employee's rights in his accrued benefit derived from his own contributions are nonforfeitable.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, maximum permitted vesting schedules for an individual account plan
citations.quote: (i) In the case of an individual account plan, a plan satisfies the requirements of this paragraph if it satisfies the requirements of clause (ii) or (iii). (ii) A plan satisfies the requirements of this clause if an employee who has completed at least 3 years of service has a nonforfeitable right to 100 percent of the employee's accrued benefit derived from employer contributions. (iii) A plan satisfies the requirements of this clause if an employee has a nonforfeitable right to a percentage of the employee's accrued benefit derived from employer contributions determined under the following table: Years of service: The nonforfeitable percentage is: 2 20 3 40 4 60 5 80 6 or more 100.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, definition of "individual account plan" / "defined contribution plan"
citations.quote: The term “individual account plan” or “defined contribution plan” means a pension plan which provides for an individual account for each participant and for benefits based solely upon the amount contributed to the participant's account, and any income, expenses, gains and losses, and any forfeitures of accounts of other participants which may be allocated to such participant's account.

expectedJSON.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the vesting rules under 29 U.S.C. § 1053(a) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs the reader's situation, and not a claim about the terms of any specific retirement plan, which can vary within what federal law permits. Two of the citations below are to different subsections of the same statutory section, 29 U.S.C. § 1053(a) — paragraph (1) (full vesting of an employee's own contributions) and paragraph (2)(B) (the two permitted maximum vesting schedules for an individual account plan) — and are disclosed together here rather than presented as independent sources. This clause states the individual-account-plan vesting schedules in § 1053(a)(2)(B), because a 401(k) is an individual account (defined contribution) plan; § 1053(a)(2)(A), a separate, slightly longer schedule (a 5-year cliff, or a 3-through-7-year graded schedule) that applies specifically to defined benefit plans, is not restated here because it does not govern a 401(k)-type account. The third citation, to 29 U.S.C. § 1002(34), a different statutory section defining "individual account plan," supports that classification and is cited as a separate, independent source rather than folded into the § 1053(a) disclosure above.
